blocks.text: The movement of substances in and out of cells is crucial for cellular functions: nutrient uptake, waste elimination, gas exchange and signal transduction. Cells rely on the plasma membrane to regulate this movement. Membrane transport mechanisms are the processes that enable a cell to maintain homeostasis, acquire nutrients, remove waste products and communicate with its environment. There are two kinds: passive transport, which requires no energy input, and active transport, which uses energy.

blocks.title: Equilibrium
blocks.text: While exchanging matter with the cell's environment, plasma membranes maintain equilibrium inside the cell as well as outside.
Passive transport
The movement of molecules across the plasma membrane without any expenditure of energy is passive transport. Its types are diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis.
Diffusion

Diffusion is the net movement of a substance (liquid or gas) from an area of higher concentration to one of lower concentration, that is along the concentration gradient. Because a cell does not expend energy when molecules diffuse across its membrane, diffusion is a type of passive transport.

blocks.alt: Three panels in time order, joined by arrows. In each, a membrane with gaps divides a space; at first blue molecules are mostly on the left and green molecules on the right; both kinds move through the gaps until, in the last panel, each kind is spread evenly on both sides.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.34: Diffusion of two types of molecules (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.34).

blocks.text: Facilitated diffusion

Some molecules are taken into or out of cells with the help of transport proteins in the plasma membrane. When a transport protein helps a substance move down its concentration gradient (from higher to lower concentration), the process is facilitated diffusion. It is also passive, because no energy is used. Its rate depends on how many transport-protein molecules are available in the membrane. The main types of transport protein involved are:

blocks.alt: A plasma membrane (phospholipid bilayer) with a transport protein spanning it. Solute molecules on one side pass through the transport protein to the other side, down their concentration gradient.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.35: Facilitated diffusion (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.35).

items: Channel proteins: these form hydrophilic channels across the membrane that allow specific molecules or ions to pass through. They can be gated or non-gated; gated channels open or close in response to specific stimuli (such as voltage changes, ligand binding or mechanical stress). Examples include ion channels (for specific ions such as Na+, K+, Ca2+ and Cl-) and aquaporins (for the rapid transport of water molecules).

Carrier proteins (transporters): these bind the specific molecule they transport, undergo a conformational change, and move the molecule across the membrane. They are highly specific and can become saturated: there is a maximum rate of transport when all carrier proteins are occupied. Examples include glucose transporters and amino acid transporters.

blocks.caption: Difference between simple and facilitated diffusion
rows: Substances move from higher to lower concentration directly through the lipid bilayer of the plasma membrane
Substances move from higher to lower concentration through specific transport proteins embedded in the plasma membrane
Passive; no energy input from the cell
Typically small, non-polar molecules such as oxygen, carbon dioxide and lipid-soluble substances
Primarily polar or charged molecules such as glucose, amino acids and ions, which cannot easily pass through the hydrophobic core of the bilayer
Depends on the concentration gradient, temperature and the permeability of the membrane
Affected by the number and availability of transport proteins; reaches a maximum when all transport proteins are saturated

blocks.text: Osmosis

The process by which water molecules diffuse across a cell membrane from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration is osmosis. Because water moves from higher to lower concentration, osmosis does not require the cell to expend energy; it is the passive transport of water. The direction of osmosis depends on the concentration of solutes on the two sides of the membrane: water always moves from a hypotonic solution (lower solute concentration) to a hypertonic solution (higher solute concentration).

blocks.title: Tonicity
blocks.text: Tonicity is the relative concentration of solutes in solutions. Hypertonic solutions have more solute; hypotonic solutions have less solute; isotonic solutions have equal concentrations of solutes.

Osmosis occurs through a selectively permeable membrane, which allows water to pass while restricting many solutes. It is crucial for maintaining cell turgor, vital for plant cells, and for balancing the internal water content of cells. The direction and rate of osmosis are influenced by the osmotic gradient and the permeability of the membrane to water. Specialised proteins called aquaporins facilitate the rapid transport of water molecules across the membrane, ensuring efficient regulation of cellular hydration and volume.

blocks.alt: A selectively permeable membrane separates a hypotonic solution (left) from a hypertonic solution (right). Each solute molecule is surrounded by a cluster of water molecules; free water molecules are more numerous on the hypotonic side. An arrow below shows the net flow of water from the hypotonic to the hypertonic side.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.36: Osmosis at molecular level (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.36).

blocks.title: Reverse osmosis
blocks.text: Reverse osmosis is a widely used technology for purifying water by removing contaminants and impurities. Unlike natural osmosis, which moves water from lower to higher solute concentration, reverse osmosis applies external pressure to push water through a semi-permeable membrane from higher to lower solute concentration. This filters out dissolved salts and other impurities, giving clean, safe drinking water. It is used in water treatment plants, desalination facilities and household purification systems.

blocks.alt: Two U-tubes, each with a semipermeable membrane at the bottom between concentrated solution with contaminants (left arm) and pure water (solvent, right arm). Osmosis: water flows from the pure water into the concentrated solution, whose level rises; the difference in level is the osmotic pressure. Reverse osmosis: applied pressure on the solution side pushes water through the membrane into the pure water, leaving the contaminants behind.
blocks.caption: Osmosis and reverse osmosis (original drawing after the diagram in the textbook's Reverse osmosis box).

blocks.text: Active transport

The movement of substances across the plasma membrane from lower concentration to higher concentration, with the expenditure of energy, is active transport. The following types occur through the plasma membrane.
Active transport through carrier proteins

In this process, carrier (transport) proteins in the plasma membrane use energy to move molecules against the concentration gradient. For example, the membranes of nerve cells have carrier proteins in the form of the sodium-potassium pump. In a resting nerve cell (one not conducting an impulse) this pump spends energy (ATP) to maintain a higher concentration of K+ and a lower concentration of Na+ inside the cell. For this purpose the pump actively moves Na+ to the outside of the cell and K+ to the inside.

blocks.alt: A plasma membrane between the outside of the cell (top) and the cytoplasm (bottom), with transport proteins in four successive states. Na+ ions bind the pump from the cytoplasm; ATP gives a phosphate (P), leaving ADP; the pump opens outward and releases Na+ outside; K+ ions from outside bind; the pump returns, losing the phosphate, and releases K+ into the cytoplasm.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.37: Active transport through carrier proteins (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.37).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Outside cell, Transport protein, Plasma membrane, Na+, K+, P, ATP, ADP, Cytoplasm.

blocks.text: Endocytosis

In endocytosis, bulky materials are moved into the cell across the plasma membrane. A portion of the plasma membrane invaginates (is depressed inwards); the material from outside is taken into the invagination and its ends seal, forming a small vesicle that detaches from the plasma membrane and moves into the cytoplasm. The two common forms are phagocytosis, in which the cell takes in solid material, and pinocytosis, in which the cell takes in liquids in the form of droplets.

blocks.title: Receptor-mediated endocytosis
blocks.text: Specific receptor proteins of the plasma membrane pick up material from outside and pinch inwards to form a vesicle. For example, liver cells have receptor proteins for cholesterol. Cholesterol circulates in the blood as low-density lipoproteins (LDLs); the receptor proteins of liver cell membranes recognise and take up LDLs from the blood by receptor-mediated endocytosis.

blocks.alt: An LDL particle (a phospholipid outer layer with proteins, carrying cholesterol inside) approaches the plasma membrane, binds receptor proteins in a pit of the membrane, and is taken into the cytoplasm inside a vesicle.
blocks.caption: Receptor-mediated endocytosis of LDL (original drawing after the diagram in the textbook's Receptor-mediated endocytosis box).
blocks.long_description: Labels: LDL particle, Phospholipid outer layer, Cholesterol, Protein, Plasma membrane, Receptor protein, Vesicle, Cytoplasm.

blocks.text: Exocytosis

Exocytosis is the process by which bulky material is exported out of the cell. The material is packed inside a membrane to form a vesicle; the vesicle moves to the plasma membrane and fuses with it, releasing its contents into the extracellular environment.

blocks.alt: (A) Endocytosis: a particle outside the cell is enclosed by an inward pocket of the plasma membrane, which pinches off as a vesicle inside the cell; the material is imported. (B) Exocytosis: vesicles with material packed inside move to the plasma membrane, fuse with it and open, so the material is exported outside the cell.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.38: (A) Endocytosis, (B) Exocytosis (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.38).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Plasma membrane, Outside of cell, Inside of cell, Material imported, Material exported, Material packed in vesicle.
